_meta.keyKnowledge: We are learning about the fundamental economic problem of scarcity — that resources are limited while wants are unlimited — and how this forces us to make choices involving trade-offs.

toLevel2.question: Scarcity in economics has no link to the gap between unlimited wants and the limited resources available.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Scarcity is defined as the gap between unlimited wants and limited resources available to meet them.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating scarcity as unrelated to that gap ignores its core meaning at this level.

toLevel2.question: Opportunity cost has no link to the choice that is given up when a person decides between two options.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best option given up when a choice is made.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating opportunity cost as unrelated to the option given up misses its core meaning.

toLevel2.question: A trade-off occurs when choosing one option means giving up something else of value at the same time.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A trade-off describes the loss of one option's value when another option is chosen instead.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: This is the standard description of a trade-off in economic study.

toLevel2.question: A government can fund every project on its list at full cost without making any choice between priorities.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Government budgets are limited, so funding every project at full cost is not possible without trade-offs.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating budgets as unlimited ignores the role of scarcity in government spending choices.

toLevel2.question: Individuals face no scarcity in everyday choices about how to spend limited time or money on competing wants.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Daily choices about limited time and money are clear examples of scarcity in everyday life.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating individuals as facing no scarcity ignores how time and money limits shape daily choices.

toLevel2.question: Businesses with limited resources must choose what to produce because they cannot make every possible product at once.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Limited resources force businesses to choose what to produce; they cannot produce every possible item.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Business scarcity is widely taught as a core example at this level.

toLevel2.question: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have managed scarce resources sustainably across many thousands of years.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples have sustainably managed scarce resources across millennia.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Sustainable management of resources by First Nations Peoples is widely documented and continues today.

toLevel2.question: The concept of scarcity applies only to government budgets and has no link to personal or business choices.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Scarcity applies to government, business, and personal choices because all face limited resources.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating scarcity as government-only ignores its role in personal and business decisions.

toLevel2.question: Opportunity cost helps decision-makers compare the value of one option against the value of the next-best option.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Comparing the value of one option against the next-best is the core function of opportunity cost.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost is widely used as a comparison tool in decision-making.

toLevel2.question: If a community chooses to build a hospital instead of a sports stadium, the stadium represents the opportunity cost.
toLevel2.correct: True
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The stadium given up to build the hospital is the opportunity cost of that decision.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: This is a recognised example of opportunity cost in community decisions.

toLevel2.question: Scarcity forces choices, but those choices never involve any trade-off between competing wants in any setting.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Scarcity forces choices that involve trade-offs because resources cannot meet every competing want at once.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating scarcity as separate from trade-offs ignores how the two ideas connect.

toLevel2.question: Every economic choice always uses every available resource without leaving any other option for any other use.
toLevel2.correct: False
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Every economic choice gives up other possible uses of the same resource, which is the trade-off.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating choices as having no other uses ignores the reality of competing wants for resources.

toLevel2.question: Which of the following best defines scarcity in economics?
toLevel2.correct: Scarcity describes the gap between limited resources and the unlimited wants people would like to satisfy
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Scarcity is the gap between limited resources and the unlimited wants people would like to satisfy.

distractors.answer: Scarcity describes a market where resources are unlimited but every consumer want is fully satisfied at all times
distractors.explanation: Resources are limited and wants exceed them, so this option contradicts the basic concept.

distractors.answer: Scarcity describes a country with no shortages and no need to make any economic choice between options
distractors.explanation: All economies face scarcity and must make choices; this option contradicts the basic concept.

distractors.answer: Scarcity describes a single rare item that is unavailable for sale at any shop in any setting
distractors.explanation: Scarcity is the broad limited-resource condition, not a single rare retail item.

toLevel2.question: What is opportunity cost?
toLevel2.correct: The next-best option that a person gives up when choosing one option over another in a decision
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Opportunity cost is the next-best option that a person gives up when making a decision.

distractors.answer: The total dollar amount written on the price tag of a product before any discount is applied at the till
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost is about the option given up, not the dollar price tag of the chosen item.

distractors.answer: The benefit of every option combined together once a person has chosen one of the available options
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost focuses on the next-best option only, not on every option combined.

distractors.answer: The cost of repeating a single decision many times over the course of one financial year
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost relates to the option given up in one decision, not repeated decisions.

toLevel2.question: Which of the following best describes a trade-off?
toLevel2.correct: A choice in which selecting one option means accepting the loss of another option's value
toLevel2.correctExplanation: A trade-off is a choice in which selecting one option means accepting the loss of another option's value.

distractors.answer: A choice that fully satisfies every competing want without any need to give anything up at all
distractors.explanation: Trade-offs always involve giving something up; this option contradicts the basic concept.

distractors.answer: A market situation in which all possible products are produced at once with no limits applied
distractors.explanation: Limits on resources prevent producing every possible product at once.

distractors.answer: A government policy that removes scarcity from every household budget across the whole nation
distractors.explanation: No policy can remove scarcity entirely; trade-offs remain part of household choices.

toLevel2.question: Why must governments make choices between competing priorities such as hospitals, schools, and roads?
toLevel2.correct: Government budgets are limited, so funding more of one priority usually means funding less of another
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Limited budgets force trade-offs between priorities; more for one usually means less for another.

distractors.answer: Government budgets are unlimited but ministers prefer to fund only the most popular projects each year
distractors.explanation: Government budgets are limited; the popularity claim does not match how scarcity works.

distractors.answer: Government budgets always grow large enough to fund every priority at full cost in any year
distractors.explanation: Budgets do not grow without limit; scarcity forces choices each year.

distractors.answer: Government budgets only fund hospitals because schools and roads receive funds from a different source
distractors.explanation: Schools and roads share the same overall budget; this option contradicts how funding works.

toLevel2.question: Which of the following is the best example of opportunity cost in a personal choice?
toLevel2.correct: A student who buys a textbook for $40 and gives up buying a concert ticket priced at $40
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Buying the textbook means giving up the concert ticket; the ticket is the opportunity cost.

distractors.answer: A student who saves $40 in cash at home and earns no interest from a basic bank account
distractors.explanation: Saving cash without interest is not a clear trade-off between two competing wants.

distractors.answer: A student who works on Saturday for $40 and pays $40 in income tax on those earnings
distractors.explanation: Tax is a deduction from earnings, not the opportunity cost of a personal choice.

distractors.answer: A student who finds $40 in a pocket and decides to spend the money on extra school stationery
distractors.explanation: Spending found money is a single choice without a clearly compared alternative.

toLevel2.question: Why are trade-offs a normal part of business decisions?
toLevel2.correct: Businesses have limited resources and must choose what to produce because they cannot produce every option
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Limited resources force businesses to choose what to produce, which means accepting trade-offs.

distractors.answer: Businesses have unlimited resources but choose to produce only the most profitable item each season
distractors.explanation: Resources are limited; profit alone does not capture the basic role of scarcity.

distractors.answer: Businesses face no scarcity and so they freely produce every product their customers ever request
distractors.explanation: All businesses face scarcity; choosing what to produce is a normal feature of business.

distractors.answer: Businesses always produce only one product across all years to avoid any choice between options
distractors.explanation: Most businesses produce more than one product over time and choose between options.

toLevel2.question: Which scenario best illustrates scarcity in personal life?
toLevel2.correct: A young person earns $30 each week and chooses between saving for a bike and spending on snacks
toLevel2.correctExplanation: $30 a week with two competing wants is a clear example of personal scarcity and trade-off.

distractors.answer: A young person finds $30 in a wallet and uses the money to buy snacks for the rest of the week
distractors.explanation: Spending found money on one thing is not a clear competing-want trade-off scenario.

distractors.answer: A young person receives a free ticket to a concert and attends the event with a friend on Saturday
distractors.explanation: A free ticket without competing wants does not show personal scarcity at work.

distractors.answer: A young person watches a film at home and enjoys the film without buying anything else after
distractors.explanation: Watching a film without purchases does not show competing wants under limited resources.

toLevel2.question: Which of the following best describes how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples manage scarce resources?
toLevel2.correct: Through long-standing sustainable practices that maintain resources for community use across many generations
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Long-standing sustainable practice maintains scarce resources for community use across generations.

distractors.answer: Through random short-term harvests that have no plan and no shared knowledge among any community members
distractors.explanation: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander resource management is planned and uses shared knowledge.

distractors.answer: Through a single shared system used identically by every nation across Australia in every region every year
distractors.explanation: Different nations have distinct practices; identical systems across Australia is incorrect.

distractors.answer: Through complete avoidance of any harvest at any time so that resources are never used by any community
distractors.explanation: Resources are used to support community life; complete avoidance is not how management works.

toLevel2.question: Which list includes only ideas central to scarcity?
toLevel2.correct: Limited resources, unlimited wants, and the choices that scarcity forces between competing options
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Limited resources, unlimited wants, and forced choices are core to the idea of scarcity.

distractors.answer: Limited resources, balanced budgets, and the bonus payments that businesses sometimes give to staff
distractors.explanation: Bonus payments are a workplace policy detail, not part of the scarcity concept itself.

distractors.answer: Unlimited resources, limited wants, and the lack of any choice between any competing options
distractors.explanation: Resources are limited and wants exceed them; this option reverses the basic concept.

distractors.answer: Random outcomes, share prices, and the colour of office buildings in major capital cities each year
distractors.explanation: Share prices and office colours have no link to the core idea of scarcity.

toLevel2.question: Which scenario best illustrates a trade-off between competing wants?
toLevel2.correct: A community deciding between a new pool and a new library when only one project can be funded this year
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Choosing between a pool and a library when only one can be funded is a clear community trade-off.

distractors.answer: A community holding a free public concert in a park that everyone in the area can attend at no cost
distractors.explanation: A free public concert is not a competing-wants choice between two limited options.

distractors.answer: A community receiving an unconditional grant that funds every requested project at full cost in one year
distractors.explanation: An unconditional grant that funds every project removes the trade-off rather than illustrating it.

distractors.answer: A community where every resident already owns every possible item they could ever wish to own at home
distractors.explanation: Universal ownership of every want would mean no scarcity; this scenario does not show a trade-off.

toLevel2.question: Why does opportunity cost matter in decision-making?
toLevel2.correct: It helps decision-makers compare the value of one option against the value of the next-best option
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Opportunity cost compares the value of one option against the next-best option in a decision.

distractors.answer: It removes every choice from a decision so that the decision-maker can simply pick any option without thought
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost informs choices; it does not remove the need to choose.

distractors.answer: It guarantees that every decision will produce the highest possible benefit for every group involved
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost informs decisions; it does not guarantee the highest benefit for every group.

distractors.answer: It applies only to government decisions and has no link to personal or business choices in any setting
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost applies to government, business, and personal decisions equally.

toLevel2.question: Which of the following best describes how scarcity links to choice?
toLevel2.correct: Limited resources force choices because not every want can be satisfied at the same time
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Limited resources force choices because not every want can be satisfied at the same time.

distractors.answer: Unlimited resources force choices because every want can already be satisfied at the same time
distractors.explanation: Unlimited resources would mean no scarcity, not forced choices.

distractors.answer: Limited resources never force any choice because resources can always be expanded with new technology
distractors.explanation: Even with new technology, resources remain limited and choices must still be made.

distractors.answer: Choices are made only when a person has no resources at all to use for any want at any time
distractors.explanation: Choices arise from limits on resources, not from a complete absence of resources.

toLevel2.sentence: Scarcity describes the gap between {{blank:1}} resources and unlimited wants, and {{blank:2}} cost is the next-best option a person gives up.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.answer: uniform
distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not the description of a constrained resource.

distractors.answer: scored
distractors.explanation: Scored describes a competition outcome, not a description of a resource limit.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.answer: uniform
distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not a category of cost in economics.

distractors.answer: fixture
distractors.explanation: Fixture is a scheduled match, not a category of cost in economics.

toLevel2.sentence: A {{blank:1}} occurs when choosing one option means giving up another option's value, and the option given up is the opportunity {{blank:2}}.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.answer: uniform
distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not a choice that involves giving something up.

distractors.answer: fixture
distractors.explanation: Fixture is a scheduled match, not a choice that involves giving something up.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.answer: uniform
distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not the value given up in a choice.

distractors.answer: season
distractors.explanation: Season is a period of competition, not the value given up in a choice.

toLevel3.question: A student choosing between a book and a concert ticket faces no trade-off because both wants can be satisfied equally.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Choosing between two competing wants under a fixed budget is a clear personal trade-off; both cannot be fully satisfied at once.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating both wants as equally satisfied ignores how a fixed budget forces a trade-off between them.

toLevel3.question: If a council chooses a new library over a new pool, the pool given up represents zero opportunity cost.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The pool given up is exactly the opportunity cost of choosing the library; it is not zero.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating the next-best option as zero misses the basic definition of opportunity cost.

toLevel3.question: Aboriginal Peoples on Country use seasonal indicators to time harvest and care so that scarce resources continue to support communities.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Seasonal harvest and care are part of long-standing sustainable resource management on Country.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Seasonal management of scarce resources by Aboriginal Peoples is widely documented and continues today.

toLevel3.question: A government that increases health spending must usually reduce or delay another spending area because budgets are limited.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Limited budgets mean increasing one area usually requires reducing or delaying another area's funding.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Budget trade-offs are widely taught as a core feature of government spending choices.

toLevel3.question: Business scarcity has no link to the choice of what to produce when raw materials, time, and labour are limited.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Limited materials, time, and labour force businesses to choose what to produce, which is scarcity at work.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating business choices as unrelated to scarcity ignores how limits drive production decisions.

toLevel3.question: Two communities comparing development proposals can ignore opportunity cost because only the chosen option matters in any decision.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Costs, benefits, and the opportunity cost of the rejected option are all weighed in development decisions.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating opportunity cost as ignorable misses its core role in fair development decisions.

toLevel3.question: If wants and resources were both unlimited, scarcity would still force every decision to involve a trade-off.
toLevel3.correct: False
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Without limits on resources, scarcity would not exist and trade-offs would not be forced by it.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: Treating scarcity as inevitable without limits misses the basic logic of the concept.

toLevel3.question: Sustainable management of resources by First Nations Peoples shows that scarce resources can support communities across many generations when treated with care.
toLevel3.correct: True
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Sustainable management across generations is a documented strength of First Nations resource care.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: First Nations sustainable practice is widely taught at this level as a strength-based example.

toLevel3.question: Mia has $40 and is choosing between a new textbook and a concert ticket. What is her opportunity cost if she buys the textbook?
toLevel3.correct: The value of the concert ticket she gives up by spending the $40 on the textbook instead
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The opportunity cost is the value of the concert ticket she gives up by buying the textbook.

distractors.answer: The dollar amount of the textbook printed on the price label at the till at the time of purchase
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost is the option given up, not the price tag of the chosen item.

distractors.answer: The total dollar amount of the textbook and the concert ticket added together at full retail price
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost focuses on the next-best option given up, not the sum of both options.

distractors.answer: The discount available on the textbook compared with its usual price during a sale week at the shop
distractors.explanation: A discount on the chosen item is not the opportunity cost of the rejected option.

toLevel3.question: A council can fund either a new library or a new sports pool with the same money. Which idea best fits the choice the council faces?
toLevel3.correct: The chosen option's cost includes the value of the option given up because budgets are limited each year
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The chosen option's full cost includes the value of the rejected option because budgets are limited.

distractors.answer: The chosen option's cost is zero because councils never face any trade-off between projects in any year
distractors.explanation: Limited budgets force trade-offs; council costs are not zero in this sense.

distractors.answer: The chosen option's cost equals the total of all council projects added together at full retail price
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost considers only the next-best option, not all projects added together.

distractors.answer: The chosen option's cost is unrelated to the rejected option because every project has its own funding
distractors.explanation: Limited budgets link projects through trade-offs; they do not have separate independent funding.

toLevel3.question: Anika reads about Aboriginal Peoples managing harvest by season. Which idea best fits the practice?
toLevel3.correct: Long-standing sustainable management that supports communities across many generations on Country
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Seasonal management is part of long-standing sustainable practice that supports communities for generations.

distractors.answer: Random short-term harvests that have no plan and no shared knowledge across any group at all
distractors.explanation: Aboriginal seasonal management is planned and uses shared knowledge.

distractors.answer: A single shared system used identically by every Aboriginal nation in Australia each year
distractors.explanation: Different nations have distinct practices; identical systems across all is incorrect.

distractors.answer: Complete avoidance of harvest so that no resources are used by any community at any time
distractors.explanation: Resources are used to support community life; complete avoidance is not how it works.

toLevel3.question: A small business has limited materials and labour. Which idea best fits its production decisions?
toLevel3.correct: The business chooses what to produce because limited resources cannot make every product at once
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Limited resources force the business to choose what to produce, which is scarcity in action.

distractors.answer: The business produces every possible item because resources expand to meet every customer request
distractors.explanation: Resources do not expand on demand; scarcity limits what can be produced.

distractors.answer: The business produces nothing at all because limited resources prevent any production from happening
distractors.explanation: Limited resources reduce, but do not eliminate, the goods a business can produce.

distractors.answer: The business decides production by random draw rather than by weighing resources and customer demand
distractors.explanation: Production decisions are usually based on weighing resources and demand, not random draws.

toLevel3.question: A government raises health spending by $1 billion. Which trade-off most directly follows under a limited budget?
toLevel3.correct: Another spending area must usually be reduced or delayed by a similar amount in the same budget cycle
toLevel3.correctExplanation: A limited budget usually means another area must be reduced or delayed when one area increases.

distractors.answer: Every other spending area also rises by $1 billion because health spending always lifts the whole budget
distractors.explanation: Limited budgets do not lift every area together; trade-offs apply.

distractors.answer: Tax revenue automatically grows by $1 billion to cover the new health spending in the same year
distractors.explanation: Tax revenue does not automatically rise to cover new spending; trade-offs are required.

distractors.answer: The new spending has no effect on any other area of the budget because health is a separate category
distractors.explanation: Budget areas are linked through scarcity; health is not separate from other spending.

toLevel3.question: Two communities are considering rival development proposals. Which step best applies trade-off thinking?
toLevel3.correct: Compare costs, benefits, and the opportunity cost of the proposal that the community ends up rejecting
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Comparing costs, benefits, and the opportunity cost of the rejected proposal is core trade-off thinking.

distractors.answer: Choose the cheaper proposal automatically without considering benefits or any other factor at all
distractors.explanation: Cheapest-only ignores benefits and opportunity cost; this is not balanced trade-off thinking.

distractors.answer: Choose the more expensive proposal automatically because higher cost always signals higher quality
distractors.explanation: More expensive does not always mean higher quality; trade-off thinking weighs benefits explicitly.

distractors.answer: Refuse to consider either proposal and leave the community with no development at all in any year
distractors.explanation: Refusing to choose avoids the trade-off rather than applying trade-off thinking.

toLevel3.question: Sam claims that 'no scarcity exists in modern Australia because shops are always full of products'. Which idea best evaluates this claim?
toLevel3.correct: Scarcity remains because resources are still limited relative to the unlimited wants of consumers
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Full shelves do not remove scarcity; resources remain limited relative to unlimited wants.

distractors.answer: Scarcity has ended because full shop shelves prove that resources fully match every consumer want
distractors.explanation: Full shelves do not mean unlimited resources; scarcity persists in modern Australia.

distractors.answer: Scarcity exists only in poor countries and never applies in any wealthy country at any time
distractors.explanation: Scarcity affects every economy, including wealthy ones; it is not limited to poor countries.

distractors.answer: Scarcity has no link to the supply of products on shop shelves in any economy at any time
distractors.explanation: Shelf supply links to scarcity; the two are connected through resource limits.

toLevel3.question: Lila is told that opportunity cost only applies to large national decisions. Which response best fits the topic?
toLevel3.correct: Opportunity cost applies to personal, business, and government decisions because all face limited resources
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Opportunity cost applies to personal, business, and government decisions because all face limits.

distractors.answer: Opportunity cost applies only to national decisions because households never face any limited resources
distractors.explanation: Households face limited resources every day; opportunity cost applies to them too.

distractors.answer: Opportunity cost applies only to business decisions because households and governments avoid trade-offs
distractors.explanation: Households and governments face trade-offs and use opportunity cost in their decisions.

distractors.answer: Opportunity cost has no link to any decision in any setting because the concept is rarely used
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost is a core economic concept used widely in many decisions.

toLevel3.question: Kofi reads about a community choosing between a hospital and a stadium. Which idea best fits this choice?
toLevel3.correct: The rejected option's value is the opportunity cost of choosing the option the community funds
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The rejected option's value is the opportunity cost of the chosen option in this community decision.

distractors.answer: The rejected option's value is zero because only the chosen option matters in the budget at the time
distractors.explanation: Rejected options have value; opportunity cost captures that value, so it is not zero.

distractors.answer: The rejected option's value is added to the chosen option's cost in every government accounting report
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost is a concept, not an accounting line in government reports.

distractors.answer: The rejected option has no link to opportunity cost because opportunity cost applies to personal choices only
distractors.explanation: Opportunity cost applies to community decisions, not only to personal ones.

toLevel3.question: Yen is told that 'a government with surplus funds faces no scarcity'. Which response best evaluates this claim?
toLevel3.correct: Even surplus governments face scarcity because future demands compete for the same limited resources
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Even with a surplus, future demands compete for limited resources; scarcity remains.

distractors.answer: Surplus governments face no scarcity because every possible demand can be funded fully each year
distractors.explanation: Demands typically exceed any surplus over time; scarcity is not removed.

distractors.answer: Surplus governments face no scarcity because future demands always disappear after the surplus year
distractors.explanation: Future demands do not disappear; scarcity persists across many years.

distractors.answer: Surplus governments face scarcity only when ministers refuse to spend any of the surplus on projects
distractors.explanation: Scarcity is structural, not caused by ministers refusing to spend.

toLevel3.question: Rosa wants to compare two business choices: producing skateboards or producing scooters. Which idea best fits her trade-off?
toLevel3.correct: The skateboards she gives up to make scooters are part of the opportunity cost of the scooter choice
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The skateboards given up to make scooters are part of the opportunity cost of the scooter choice.

distractors.answer: The skateboards she gives up to make scooters have no link to opportunity cost in any business decision
distractors.explanation: Rejected production is the opportunity cost of the chosen production.

distractors.answer: The skateboards she gives up to make scooters add to the total revenue from making scooters in any year
distractors.explanation: Rejected production is not added to revenue; revenue comes from items actually sold.

distractors.answer: The skateboards she gives up to make scooters are unrelated to scarcity because production is unlimited
distractors.explanation: Production faces resource limits; scarcity links directly to this trade-off.

toLevel3.question: Amir reads that Aboriginal Peoples manage scarce resources sustainably across generations. Which idea best fits this practice?
toLevel3.correct: Long-standing knowledge systems that maintain scarce resources for community use over many generations
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Long-standing knowledge systems maintain scarce resources for community use across many generations.

distractors.answer: Random short-term harvests that have no plan and no link to community wellbeing across generations
distractors.explanation: Aboriginal management is planned and supports communities across generations.

distractors.answer: A single shared system used identically by every nation in Australia in every region in every year
distractors.explanation: Different nations have distinct practices; identical systems across all is incorrect.

distractors.answer: Complete avoidance of any use of resources so that nothing is harvested by any community at any time
distractors.explanation: Resources are used to support community life; complete avoidance is not how management works.

toLevel3.sentence: A government with a {{blank:1}} budget must usually reduce or delay another area to increase {{blank:2}} on health or education.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.answer: uniform
distractors.explanation: Uniform is clothing, not a description of a constrained budget.

distractors.answer: scored
distractors.explanation: Scored describes a competition outcome, not a description of a constrained budget.

blanks.correctExplanation: This option fits the sentence and matches the topic idea being tested.

distractors.answer: uniforming
